patient_case.prompt_question: A 15-year-old girl with primary amenorrhea, absent secondary sexual characteristics, and an elevated FSH level (38 mIU/mL) is evaluated. Her mother and older sister had menarche at ages 13 and 14, respectively. She is athletically active with a normal BMI. The question asks which diagnostic test should be done next.
patient_case.note: This prompt originates from a clinical scenario; diagnosis or management is to be inferred.

branch.condition: Analyze each option based on pubertal development, hormone levels, and potential etiologies of primary amenorrhea
branch.interpretation: Comparison of each option against the clinical scenario of hypergonadotropic hypogonadism

diagnostic_options.description: Evaluation for enzymatic defects related to steroid synthesis, often associated with congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
evidence_for: Relevant in adrenal hyperplasia cases with ambiguous genitalia or virilization.
evidence_against: Patient has no signs of virilization or adrenal dysfunction; the presentation is more consistent with gonadal dysgenesis leading to hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.

diagnostic_options.description: Assesses pituitary response and is more useful in cases of delayed puberty with low gonadotropins.
evidence_for: Can help differentiate central from peripheral causes of amenorrhea.
evidence_against: Elevated FSH already indicates a primary ovarian issue (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism), making this test unnecessary.

diagnostic_options.description: Chromosomal analysis to evaluate for genetic causes such as Turner syndrome or other gonadal dysgenesis.
evidence_for: Elevated FSH and absent pubertal development point to primary ovarian failure; karyotyping is indicated to assess for chromosomal anomalies like Turner syndrome.
evidence_against: None significant in this clinical context.

diagnostic_options.description: Measurement of LH can be useful to further classify reproductive hormonal status.
evidence_for: May provide additional information on gonadotropin levels.
evidence_against: Given the already elevated FSH, LH measurement would not alter the management or point to a specific diagnosis.

reasoning_tree.conclusion: The most appropriate next diagnostic step is karyotyping to evaluate for chromosomal abnormalities, such as Turner syndrome, in a patient with primary amenorrhea and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.
